disclaimer: WHERE, NOT WHY — every number on this page is descriptive. Geography correlates everything with everything; the survey shows where things coincide and never claims to know why.
computed: 2026-11-05 (v0.6: the never-correlated layers — faith, company, the sorting — run through pipeline/correlate.py v06 with nationwide, within-state, and population-band checks; two shipped, four rejected and recorded in correlate.py). Earlier: 2026-07-07 v0.5 review.
method_root: pipeline/correlate.py — county centroids decoded from the counties TopoJSON; distances by haversine; correlations are Pearson on log-transformed values. All inputs are the survey's own staged, provenance-tracked layers.

findings.title: Poisoned Ground, Poisoned People
findings.body: Counties within 15 km of a Superfund NPL site average 21.6 overdose deaths per 100k. Counties 75 km or farther average 11.9. Where we buried the industry, the epidemic runs nearly twice as hot.
findings.method: 3,012 counties with 2024 CDC crude rates; county centroid to nearest of 1,840 NPL sites; bucket means ≤15 km (n=503) vs ≥75 km (n=665); Pearson r(rate, log distance) = −0.21. Industrial-legacy regions confound both variables.

findings.title: The Folklore Fails
findings.body: This survey's own essay assumed despair pools farthest from the money. The data disagrees: counties within 25 km of a Fortune 500 headquarters average 21.8 deaths per 100k against 14.1 in counties 150 km or farther. The epidemic is Appalachian and metropolitan at once — Baltimore holds one of the five worst rates in the nation. The essay has been corrected to match the data.
findings.method: Same county set; distance to nearest of 500 headquarters; ≤25 km (n=195) vs ≥150 km (n=1,099); r(rate, log distance) = −0.20. Crude rates run higher in older urban counties; headquarters proxy metros.

findings.title: Half the Dying Happens Near the Network
findings.statLabel: of fatal crashes within 50 km of the network
findings.body: More than half of 2023's fatal crashes happened within 50 km of an Amazon logistics facility; the median crash sits 47 km from the network. The corridors that promise tomorrow's package collect today's toll.
findings.method: 37,640 located crashes; distance to nearest of 314 facilities. For scale: the median county centroid sits 127 km from the network, so crashes run systematically closer than the country's geography does. Both follow population and interstates.

findings.title: The Cloud Landed Nowhere New
findings.statLabel: of data-center cells already held remembered births
findings.body: Nearly every quarter-degree cell that holds a data center already held the birthplace of someone the world remembers. Genius pooled in the same places for five thousand years; the machines moved into the same rooms.
findings.method: 0.25° cells over the contiguous US; 8,374 cells hold memory or data centers; r(log births, log data centers) = 0.27. Population underlies both — read this as continuity, not cause.

findings.title: The Strongest Correlation Here Is Meaningless
findings.body: Sightings correlate with data centers more strongly than memory does — because both simply follow people. This card is the warning label for every other card on this page: geography correlates everything with everything. The survey shows where. It never proves why.
findings.method: 0.25° US cells, log–log Pearson across 9,484 cells. Deliberately included as the epistemic control for the whole findings page.

findings.title: Memory Moved West for 4,300 Years — Then Turned
findings.statLabel: drift of the center of remembered birth
findings.body: The mean longitude of remembered births: 34°E in antiquity — the eastern Mediterranean. 18°E medieval. 2°E early modern. 5°W industrial. Then the drift stops, and in the 20th century it ticks back east as Asia re-enters the record. Drag the era scrubber and watch it happen.
findings.method: 1,654,726 dated, located births; count-weighted mean longitude per era bucket: 34.3°E → 17.8°E → 2.1°E → 4.8°W → 4.6°W.

findings.title: Half the Worst Counties, Five States
findings.body: Fifty of the hundred highest overdose rates in America sit in Kentucky, West Virginia, Ohio, Virginia, and Tennessee — states that hold barely a sixth of the nation's rated counties. The seam of the epidemic follows the seam of the coal.
findings.method: Top-100 counties by 2024 crude rate; the five states hold 15.8% of rated counties but 50% of the top hundred.

findings.title: The Empty Chair
findings.statLabel: overdose rate where cross-class friendship is thinnest
findings.body: Counties in the bottom fifth of economic connectedness — where poor and rich residents almost never befriend each other — average 22.9 overdose deaths per 100k. Counties in the top fifth average 9.8. The strongest county-level correlation this survey has measured is about who knows whom.
findings.method: 2,897 counties with both 2024 CDC crude overdose rates and Social Capital Atlas economic connectedness; Pearson r = −0.33; quintile means 22.9 vs 9.8. Connectedness is entangled with income, education, and rurality — this card measures coincidence, not rescue.

findings.title: The Sorting Leaves the Pews Behind
findings.statLabel: religious adherence where households arrive fastest
findings.body: The fifth of counties gaining households fastest average 444 religious adherents per 1,000 residents. The fifth losing them fastest average 524. The pattern holds inside states, not just between the Sun Belt and the old cores. One plain explanation is mechanical: congregations are counted where their buildings stand, and buildings lag behind new subdivisions. The survey shows the coincidence, not which explanation is right.
findings.method: 2,841 counties with IRS SOI net household migration (2022–23) scaled per 1,000 residents and 2020 U.S. Religion Census adherence (counties above 1,000 per 1k excluded as cross-county draw). Pearson r = −0.20, Spearman −0.19; within-state (state-demeaned) r = −0.20. Quintile means 524 vs 444. Adherence predates the migration year.

findings.title: The Altar That Was Really a Map
findings.statLabel: the Lutheran gap, nationwide vs inside the same states
findings.body: Counties whose largest tradition is Lutheran average 6.2 overdose deaths per 100k; non-denominational counties average 23.8. A headline writes itself. Then compare counties inside the same states and the gap nearly closes: 5.7 against 7.4. Lutheran counties are Upper Midwest counties, and the Upper Midwest sits far from the epidemic's seams. The spurious card warns that everything follows people. This one warns that everything follows region.
findings.method: Largest tradition family per county from the 2020 U.S. Religion Census; 2024 CDC crude overdose rates. Nationwide means: Lutheran 6.2 (n=163), Baptist 19.6 (n=1,047), non-denominational 23.8 (n=311). Within the nine states holding at least five Lutheran-plurality and five other counties, weighted means 5.7 vs 7.4. Adherence rate itself vs overdose: r = −0.19 nationwide, −0.10 within states — rejected as a finding.
